one_liner: Single-header C stackful asymmetric coroutines with a hand-written assembly switch, about 40x cheaper than ucontext on x86-64 Linux.
what_it_does: Lua-style asymmetric coroutines for C (and C++): mco_create/mco_resume/mco_yield/mco_destroy, plus a small LIFO storage buffer (mco_push/mco_pop) for passing values across yield and resume. It is one header (define MINICORO_IMPL in one .c file) with backends for x86-64, i686, ARM/ARM64, RISC-V, ucontext, Windows fibers and WebAssembly (Emscripten fibers or Binaryen asyncify). It replaces getcontext/makecontext/swapcontext with a different, coroutine-object API rather than a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: The x86-64 SysV switch (_mco_switch) is 16 instructions: it stores rip/rsp/rbp/rbx/r12-r15 into the from-buffer, loads them from the to-buffer and jumps; it saves no signal mask, so there is no sigprocmask syscall as in glibc swapcontext. The Windows variant also saves xmm6-xmm15 and the TIB stack fields. Init only lays out a stack and a context buffer (inspired by Mike Pall's Lua Coco).
when_to_use: Generators, iterators or scripting-language coroutines in C where you resume and yield millions of times and ucontext's syscall per switch dominates
Embedding coroutines in a game engine or language runtime that must run on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, RISC-V and the web from one file
Projects that need a public-domain/MIT-0 single header with custom allocator hooks and ASan/TSan/Valgrind support
Many coroutines with uneven stack use, with MCO_USE_VMEM_ALLOCATOR (about 8 KB physical per coroutine for 100k coroutines with ~2 MB reserved, per README)
when_not_to_use: C++ code that throws exceptions across a yield or relies on destructors of a suspended coroutine: the README says to avoid exceptions and to resume to completion for RAII (issue #20 asks for unwinding support, not provided)
When you need symmetric transfer, a scheduler, I/O integration or work-stealing: it is only a switch primitive (compare libdill, libgo, Marl)
If you need proof it beats Boost.Context, libco or libaco: the README only compares against its own ucontext and fiber backends
OpenBSD amd64 (open issue #27, crash) and WASI SDK with the asyncify backend (README says it fails)
Deep recursion in coroutines with default stacks: 56 KB default, overflow is only detected after the fact at yield and is otherwise undefined

integration.dependencies: none (libc; ucontext or Windows fibers only on fallback paths)
integration.min_toolchain: C89 compiler for the library; thread_local/_Thread_local/__thread needed for multithreaded use
integration.platforms: x86-64 and i686 (Linux, macOS, Windows), ARM/ARM64 (Android, iOS, macOS, Raspberry Pi), RISC-V rv32/rv64, WebAssembly via Emscripten; ucontext fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: mco_coro objects are not thread safe (guard with a mutex); the current-coroutine pointer is thread_local unless MCO_NO_MULTITHREAD
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces swapcontext-based coroutines but with its own mco_* API; mco_init/mco_uninit allow caller-allocated storage

gotchas: The README cycle numbers come from tests/benchmark.c built with -O3 -flto -march=native -DNDEBUG -DMCO_NO_MULTITHREAD (tests/Makefile), so the 9-cycle switch excludes the thread_local lookup of the default build; cycles are rdtsc reference ticks, not core cycles

The switch returns with an indirect jmp rather than ret, which defeats the return-stack predictor; a minicoro-derived fork (PavelGuzenfeld/ucoro #11) measured about 3x Boost.Context before fixing this
Do not use thread_local inside coroutine bodies if coroutines migrate between threads: the compiler may cache the TLS address
The x86-64 SysV switch does not save MXCSR or the x87 control word (Boost.Context does), so code that changes FP rounding modes inside a coroutine leaks the setting to the resumer
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick minicoro over libaco or libco when you need one portable, permissively licensed header that also covers Windows, ARM, RISC-V and WebAssembly; pick libdill or libgo when you want a scheduler and I/O on top, and Neco/llco if you want a similar single-file C design with a runtime included.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table on an Intel Core i7-8750H: x86-64 Linux assembly backend 9 cycles per switch, 31 cycles init, 14 uninit, versus 352/383/14 for the library's own ucontext backend; on Windows 33/74/14 versus Windows fibers 69/10564/11167. The harness is tests/benchmark.c (10M resume/yield pairs timed with rdtsc, 100k init/uninit on pre-allocated memory), gcc with -O3 -flto -march=native -DMCO_NO_MULTITHREAD; gcc version not stated.
